learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Secure File Uploads.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 14: File Upload, Download, and Storage Security. It builds practical understanding of Secure File Uploads with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Secure File Uploads addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Validate file size and content, generate server-side names, store uploads outside executable/public paths, isolate parsers, and authorize every private download.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Secure File Uploads can be understood through this sequence: Receive file reference → Validate content + size → Isolate storage → Authorize retrieval. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 100.1 Upload workflows and threat modeling; 100.2 Allowlisted extensions and content types; 100.3 File signatures and content inspection; 100.4 Filename normalization and safe generated names; 100.5 File size and resource limits; 100.6 Malware scanning and quarantine workflows; 100.7 Storage isolation and execution prevention. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Validate file size and content, generate server-side names, store uploads outside executable/public paths, isolate parsers, and authorize every private download.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Secure File Uploads
content_blocks.code:
MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES = 5 * 1024 * 1024
ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS = {".png", ".jpg", ".pdf"}

# Also inspect content, generate a server-side filename,
# store outside the web root, and authorize downloads.
content_blocks.expected_output: Files larger than 5 MiB or with a non-allowlisted extension should be rejected by the corresponding server-side checks.
content_blocks.run_instructions: A filename extension and declared Content-Type are not proof of file type. Quarantine and isolate complex parsers and treat downloads as private by default.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Validate file size and content, generate server-side names, store uploads outside executable/public paths, isolate parsers, and authorize every private download. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Secure File Uploads”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Secure File Uploads in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Secure File Uploads is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Validate file size and content, generate server-side names, store uploads outside executable/public paths, isolate parsers, and authorize every private download.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
